title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
text:
Story 1 · Histoire 1
The Scent No One Could See
L’odeur invisible

Transition, ~5 sec. Timing target for Story 1: ~9 minutes.

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
text:
1879 · Sérignan, France
A naturalist keeps a newly-emerged female moth caged in his study. That night, dozens of males pour in through the open window.

How does a male moth find a female — kilometers away, in total darkness?
Comment un papillon mâle trouve-t-il une femelle, à des kilomètres, dans le noir total ?

⏳ Think, 60 seconds — talk to your neighbor.

Read the setting, then the question, then actually pause ~60 sec. Let a couple of students guess before revealing. This naturalist is Jean-Henri Fabre — save the name for the reveal.

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
section: Jean-Henri Fabre rules out sight and sound
text:
Jean-Henri Fabre rules out sight and sound

The night was heavily overcast and pitch dark, and the female made no sound — ruling out sight and hearing
He moved her into a sealed, airtight box → no males arrived, even with the box left in plain view — his cleanest result
He surrounded her with naphthalene (mothballs) to mask her scent → the males found her anyway
His antennae-removal test was murkier: clipped and unclipped “control” males both stopped returning after a night or two — most likely because adult moths only live 2–3 days, not because of the antennae


“It must be an odor — one we cannot perceive.”


Fabre, French naturalist, working at his home. The sealed-box result is the strongest evidence — lead with that if time is short. The antennae story is a nice honesty-in-science moment: even Fabre’s own experiment was ambiguous, and he said so himself. Bonus fact if there’s time: he first wondered if the female used a kind of “wireless telegraphy” (electromagnetic waves) before the smell explanation.

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
section: 80 years later, a Nobel laureate takes the case
text:
80 years later, a Nobel laureate takes the case

1939 — Adolf Butenandt wins the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, for isolating human sex hormones. Nothing to do with insects — yet.
He turns to Fabre’s 80-year-old puzzle: what exactly is the female silkworm moth’s scent?
It takes his team 20 years to gather enough material to identify it.

20 years · over 500,000 moths — for a few milligrams of pure substance

Nice twist: he already had science’s highest prize, for completely different work, before starting this 20-year side quest.

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
text:
Quick pause

Today, could we do this with just one moth?
Aujourd’hui, pourrait-on le faire avec un seul papillon ?

⏳ 30 seconds.

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
section: From 500,000 moths to one living antenna
text:
From 500,000 moths to one living antenna

GC-EAD (1975) — invented in Switzerland — wires a living insect antenna up as a detector on a gas chromatograph
The insect itself “tells you” which compound it can smell, peak by peak
Paired with GC-MS to confirm the exact molecular structure, from a trace air sample

What took Butenandt 20 years now takes an afternoon.

GC-EAD = gas chromatography-electroantennographic detection, invented by Arn, Städler & Rauscher. End of Story 1 (~9 min total).

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
text:
Story 2 · Histoire 2
Why Would a Plant Call for Help?
Pourquoi une plante appellerait-elle à l’aide ?

Transition, ~5 sec. Can callback to an opening “you are a plant” activity if used. Timing target for Story 2: ~9 minutes.

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
text:
Remember being a plant?
For a century, scientists looked at plant chemicals like nicotine, caffeine, and morphine, and mostly called them one thing: waste.

Why might they have thought that?
Pourquoi le pensaient-ils, selon vous ?

⏳ Think, 45 seconds — talk to your neighbor.

Let students guess — common answers: “they don’t help the plant grow,” “random byproducts of metabolism.” Both reasonable, both wrong — that’s the point.

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
text:
The “waste” assumption

Plants make thousands of chemically odd compounds
None seemed necessary for growth, photosynthesis, or reproduction
Biochemists’ default explanation: leftover metabolic “junk”


Set up the wrong idea clearly before knocking it down — that’s the whole rhetorical structure of this story.

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
text:
Quick pause
Deterring a herbivore is passive defense — make yourself less tasty and wait.

What would ACTIVE defense look like — a plant that fights back by calling in help?
À quoi ressemblerait une défense active — une plante qui appelle à l’aide ?

⏳ 60 seconds — this one tends to need more thinking time.

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
text:
Turlings, Tumlinson & Lewis, 1990

A caterpillar bites into a maize seedling
Within hours, the plant releases a specific blend of terpenoid volatiles
A parasitic wasp (Cotesia) follows that scent straight to the caterpillar — and lays its eggs inside it

The plant doesn’t just defend itself — it recruits a bodyguard.

This is the HIPV (herbivore-induced plant volatile) discovery — the foundational tritrophic-interaction paper.

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
text:
A tradition built right here
This discovery became the HIPV research tradition — herbivore-induced plant volatiles and tritrophic interactions — that Ted Turlings later built at the University of Neuchâtel.

Local pride moment — UniNE is where this research tradition lives on. Good bridge into Story 3. End of Story 2 (~9 min total).

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
text:
Story 3 · Histoire 3
When a Flower Lies
Quand une fleur ment

Transition, ~5 sec. Timing target for Story 3: ~9 minutes.

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
text:
1927 · Australia
An amateur naturalist, Edith Coleman, notices something strange about the orchids in her garden.

What if a flower didn’t need nectar or bright color — what if it could impersonate an insect instead?
Et si une fleur pouvait imiter un insecte, plutôt que d’offrir du nectar ?

⏳ Think, 45 seconds — talk to your neighbor.

Let a few guesses land before revealing — “impersonate” is the key word to plant in their minds.

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
text:
Edith Coleman, 1927

Cryptostylis orchids, in Australia, are pollinated by only one visitor: male ichneumonid wasps
The males attempt to mate with the flower itself
No reward is offered — the flower is simply mistaken for a mate


Coleman was an amateur naturalist, not an academic scientist — nice detail for who gets to make discoveries.

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
text:
Bertil Kullenberg, from 1948

Spends over a decade studying Mediterranean Ophrys orchids
Shows the flowers chemically mimic a female bee’s own sex pheromone
Males attempt to mate with the flower — and carry pollen away in the process

This is chemical mimicry, not just visual disguise.

Ophrys = the bee orchid genus. Distinguish from Story 1’s Bombyx moth pheromone — same concept, opposite direction (flower faking insect, not insect faking insect).

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
text:
Quick pause

If you were a flower faking a pheromone, how close would the copy need to be to actually fool the insect?
À quel point la copie chimique devrait-elle être fidèle pour tromper l’insecte ?

⏳ 30 seconds.

Push toward “nearly identical, compound-for-compound” as the intuition, then confirm it on the next slide.

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
text:
GC-MS confirms it

Modern chemical analysis compares orchid scent blends to the real insect pheromone
In several species, the match is nearly compound-for-compound

Deception, written in chemistry.

Same analytical toolkit as Story 1 — start planting the seed that all three stories share this technology. End of Story 3 (~9 min total).

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
text: Synthesis · Synthèse

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
section: All three stories — unlocked by the same tools
text:
All three stories — unlocked by the same tools

GC-MS separates and identifies compounds from tiny, complex mixtures
GC-EAD lets an insect’s own antenna point to the biologically relevant ones
From Fabre’s moths, to Turlings’ maize, to Kullenberg’s orchids — the same chemistry toolkit cracked every case


Explicit callback tying the technology thread across all three stories. ~1 min.

title: Three Mysteries in Chemical Ecology
text:

What do you think is still a mystery today?
⏳ Quick share — a few volunteers.
Merci — welcome to the course.
Prof. Pengjuan Zu

Genuine open question, let a few students answer, no need to resolve it. Then close: “Merci — welcome to the course.” ~2-3 min. Total session: ~30 min.
